note: Born of Chaos with her brother Erebus (Theogony 123); in Hyginus from Chaos and Caligo, Mist (Fabulae preface)
Out of Chaos came Erebus and black Night (Theogony 123); in Hyginus from Chaos and Caligo, Mist (Fabulae preface)
The first darkness, twin-born of Chaos in Hesiod; born in one brood from Chaos and Caligo in Hyginus
Night lay in love with Erebus and bore Aether and Day (Theogony 124–125); Hyginus makes the union mother of the Parcae as well (moirai-parentage dispute)
Borne by Gaia alone, equal to herself, to cover her on every side (Theogony 126–128); Hyginus instead makes the Sky a child of Aether and Dies, who are outside the roster
By the sky she herself had borne, mother of the Titans, the Cyclopes and the Hundred-Handers
In love with Tartarus through golden Aphrodite she bore Typhoeus, her youngest child (Theogony 820–822)
Aphrodite's winged and unruly son only in later poets; in Hesiod, Eros is primordial and unbegotten, arising beside Chaos, Gaia and Tartarus
Youngest and most terrible of the brood of Uranus and Gaia
Eldest of the Titan children of Uranus and Gaia; in Homer (Iliad 14) Oceanus is instead the primeval origin from whom the gods are sprung
First of the children Gaia bore to starry Uranus; Homer knows him not as a Titan son but as the genesis of the gods
Lovely Tethys, youngest of the Titanides in Hesiod; in Homer she is 'mother Tethys', a primeval mother at the origin of the gods
Daughter of Uranus and Gaia in Hesiod and Apollodorus; no Titan daughter at all in Homer's Iliad 14
Borne to starry Uranus among the elder Titans (Theogony 132–138)
Sister-wife pair among the Titans — paired with the consort edge
Eldest and youngest of the Titan brood; Oceanus alone held back when the brothers fell on Uranus (Apollodorus)
Homer remembers the two together, sitting in the sunless depths with Tartarus all around them (Iliad 8.478–481)
Sister-wife pair — paired with the consort edge per the incest convention
King in his father's place, Cronus wed his sister Rhea, who bore the six eldest Olympians; Homer: Il. 15.187 ('three brothers... begotten of Cronus, and born of Rhea')
Parents of the three thousand Rivers and three thousand Oceanid nymphs; in Homer the primeval couple from whom the gods are sprung, who nursed Hera in their halls
Mother: the Oceanid Clymene (Hesiod, Hyginus) or her sister Asia (Apollodorus) — outside the roster
Mother: the Oceanid Clymene (Hesiod, Hyginus) or Asia (Apollodorus) — outside the roster
Full brothers among the four sons of Iapetus, with Menoetius and Epimetheus
Youngest child, saved from his father's belly by the trick of a swaddled stone
Rhea bore him in secret and hid him in a cave on Crete
Swallowed at birth like each of Rhea's children
In Homer, Rhea handed her to Oceanus and Tethys to be reared while Zeus warred on Cronus (Iliad 14.302–303)
One of the three brothers begotten of Cronus and born of Rhea (Iliad 15.187–188)
Second-born of the six, swallowed straight from the womb
Firstborn of Cronus and Rhea — first swallowed and last set free; Hyginus' list of Saturn's children keeps her precedence
One of the three brothers begotten of Cronus and born of Rhea (Iliad 15.187–188)
Eldest and youngest of the six Cronids — 'first and last' once Cronus disgorged his children in reverse order
Both sister and wife of Zeus — paired with the consort edge per the incest convention
On the strength of the lots, Poseidon insists he is Zeus's equal in honor (Iliad 15.187–193)
His last and lasting wife (Theogony 921), mother of Hebe, Eileithyia and Ares

Born fully armed from Zeus' head after he swallowed her pregnant mother, his first wife the Oceanid Metis (Theogony 886–900, 924–926); in Homer she is Zeus' own child, no mother ever named — Homer: Il. 5.875–880
Libyan tradition: daughter of Poseidon and Lake Tritonis, her sea-grey eyes inherited from her father (Description of Greece 1.14.6)
Son of Zeus and the Titaness Leto, born on Delos
Born second of the twins, his newborn sister turning midwife (Apollodorus); four days out of the cradle he avenged his mother on Python
Daughter of Zeus and the Titaness Leto, twin of Apollo
Brought forth first on Delos, then midwife at her twin brother's birth (Apollodorus)
The archer twins of Zeus and Leto, born together on Delos
Least welcome of Olympus' children at his father's knee — 'most hateful to me of all gods' (Iliad 5.890)
Borne by Hera to Zeus with Hebe and Eileithyia (Theogony 921–923)
Full brothers only in Homer, where Hephaestus is son of Zeus and Hera; in Hesiod Hera bore Hephaestus alone, making them half-brothers
Born of the sea-foam around Uranus' severed flesh (Theogony 188–206)
Daughter of Zeus and Dione (Iliad 5.370; Bibliotheca 1.3.1)
In Hesiod and Apollodorus Hera bore him entirely alone, without a father, in rivalry over Athena's birth; in Homer he is the son of both Zeus and Hera
Father only in Homer (Iliad 1.577–579; Odyssey 8.312); Hesiod and Apollodorus give him no father at all
Mother: the Pleiad Maia, daughter of Atlas, who bore him in a cave of Mount Cyllene — outside the roster; Homer: Od. 8.335 ('Hermes, son of Zeus'), Od. 14.435 (son of Maia)
Mother: the mortal Semele, daughter of Cadmus (no roster node), incinerated by Zeus' unveiled glory; the unborn child was sewn into Zeus' thigh
Orphic tradition reported by Hyginus (Fabulae 167): Liber first born of Jove and Proserpina, dismembered by the Titans, conceived again from Semele — the god with two mothers
Zeus came to the bed of all-nourishing Demeter, and she bore him white-armed Persephone (Theogony 912)
Her mother's grief at the abduction withered the world's crops — the mythic root of the seasons
Carried her off with Zeus' connivance to reign as queen of the dead; the abduction site and her yearly term below are disputed (persephone-abduction-details, persephone-split-year)
His wife in the song of Demodocus (Odyssey 8) and in Ovid's tale of the net; in the Iliad his wife is Charis, in Hesiod Aglaia, youngest of the Graces
The affair Helios exposed and Hephaestus snared in an unbreakable net; in Hesiod she bore Ares Phobos, Deimos and Harmonia (Theogony 933–937)
Joined in love with the lord of the aegis, Leto bore the archer twins Apollo and Artemis; Homer: Il. 14.327 (named in Zeus' catalogue of loves), Il. 1.9 (Apollo 'son of Leto and Zeus')
Arcadian tale from Thelpusa: he covered her as a stallion while she grazed as a mare among the herds of Oncius, an unwilling union; she bore the horse Arion and Despoina
Forced his father to disgorge the swallowed children and, after the ten-year Titanomachy, thrust Cronus down beneath the earth and the unresting sea
Alone dared answer Gaia's call: from ambush he reaped his father's manhood with the adamantine sickle
Tricked Zeus over the portions at Mecone, stole fire in a fennel stalk, and was bound in the Caucasus with an eagle at his ever-regrowing liver
Sat out the Titanomachy; through his counsels his daughter Styx came first of all to Zeus' side and was honored for it (Theogony 389–403)
Took the newborn to nurse in a Cretan cave, counselled the freeing of the Cyclopes, and prompted the gods to urge Zeus to kingship (Theogony 881–885)
When the Titans had been driven from heaven she bore Typhoeus by Tartarus to challenge the new order; the motive of anger is explicit in Apollodorus
Hunted the pregnant Titaness over the whole earth before the twins' birth on Delos; in Hyginus she decreed Latona give birth only where the sun never shone
The contest for Attica in the days of Cecrops: his well of sea-water against her first olive tree, judged for Athena
Night conceived Aether by Erebus (Theogony 123–125); Hyginus instead makes Aether a sibling of Night
Born from Chaos and Caligo alongside Night, Day and Erebus (Fabulae preface)
Night conceived Day by Erebus (Theogony 123–125); Hyginus instead makes Day a sibling of Night
Born from Chaos and Caligo alongside Night, Erebus and Aether (Fabulae preface)
The paired brightnesses of upper air and day
The twin bearers who carry Sarpedon home to Lycia in Iliad 16
Their children include the Horae and, in this genealogy, the three Moirai
Last-named of Iapetus' sons in Hesiod (Theogony 507–514); also his son in Bibliotheca 1.2.3 and Fabulae, preface
Borne by the Oceanid Clymene (Theogony 507–514); Hyginus' preface keeps Clymene as the mother
To Iapetus and Asia were born Atlas, Prometheus, Epimetheus and Menoetius (Bibliotheca 1.2.3)
Theogony 507–511; Bibliotheca 1.2.3 — Hyginus' preface omits Menoetius from Iapetus' children entirely
Clymene bore very glorious Menoetius (Theogony 507–511); Hyginus keeps Clymene but drops Menoetius from the list
Clymene bore clever Prometheus, full of various wiles (Theogony 507–514); Fabulae, preface
Clymene bore him a stout-hearted son, Atlas (Theogony 507–511); Fabulae, preface
Forethought and Afterthought, sons of Iapetus (Theogony 507–514; Bibliotheca 1.2.3; Fabulae, preface)
Hyginus' preface omits Menoetius from the brothers
Struck with a smoking thunderbolt for his mad presumption and pride (Theogony 514–516); in the battle with the Titans (Bibliotheca 1.2.3) — see menoetius-punishment for where he fell
Named in the catalogue of Oceanids (Theogony 351); 'daughter of Ocean' at Theogony 507–508
Among the daughters Tethys bore to Oceanus (Theogony 346–366)
Iapetus took to wife the neat-ankled maid Clymene and went up with her into one bed (Theogony 507–508); paired in Hyginus' preface
In the Oceanid catalogue (Theogony 359); first of the Oceanids born to Ocean and Tethys (Bibliotheca 1.2.2)
To Iapetus and Asia were born his four sons (Bibliotheca 1.2.3); in Hesiod and Hyginus his consort is Clymene instead
Both daughters of Tethys and Oceanus in the catalogue (Theogony 346–366) — rival mothers of the same four sons across authors
Moulded of earth at Zeus's command, with the voice and strength of human kind (Theogony 571–572; Works and Days 60–64); in Hyginus, Vulcan shapes the clay and Minerva gives the soul (Fabulae 142)

Hesiod has him take the gift Hermes brought, never calling her wife (Works and Days 84–89); the marriage is explicit in Hyginus (Fabulae 142) and implied by Pyrrha's birth in Apollodorus (Bibliotheca 1.7.2)
Daughter of Epimetheus and Pandora (Bibliotheca 1.7.2; Fabulae 142) — Ovid names only the father
Bibliotheca 1.7.2; Prometheus son of Iapetus begat goodly Deucalion (Argonautica 3.1086–1087); 'Promethides' (Metamorphoses 1.390)
Husband and wife who outride the flood together (Bibliotheca 1.7.2; Metamorphoses 1.313–415; Fabulae 153)
Deucalion had children by Pyrrha, first Hellen — 'whose father some say was Zeus' (Bibliotheca 1.7.2)
A minority variant in Apollodorus ('some say', Bibliotheca 1.7.2); flatly among the sons of Jove in Hyginus (Fabulae 155)
Bibliotheca 1.7.2; 'Hellen by Pyrrha, daughter of Epimetheus' (Fabulae 155)
Ocean and Tethys had a son Inachus (Bibliotheca 2.1.1); among the Rivers of Hyginus' preface
'Melia, daughter of Ocean' — her mother is never named (Bibliotheca 2.1.1)
A bare parentage formula, never called a marriage: of him and Melia were born Phoroneus and Aegialeus (Bibliotheca 2.1.1)
Bibliotheca 2.1.1; Fabulae 143; in Pausanias the father is the river itself, not a man (Description of Greece 2.15.5)
Bibliotheca 2.1.1 — Hyginus instead names Argia, Inachus' own sister (Fabulae 143)
Testified — or, with Cephisus and Asterion, judged — that the land of Argos was Hera's (Bibliotheca 2.1.4; Description of Greece 2.15.5, 2.22.4)

For siding with Hera Poseidon dried up even the springs (Bibliotheca 2.1.4); in Pausanias the rivers' waters vanished so the Inachus flows only after rain (Description of Greece 2.15.5) — or, in the rival Argive tale, he flooded the country (2.22.4)
Son of Jupiter/Zeus and Pluto/Plouto (Fabulae 82; Description of Greece 2.22.3)
Son of Jupiter/Zeus and Pluto/Plouto (Fabulae 82; Description of Greece 2.22.3)
Tantalus slaughtered Pelops before his restoration (Epitome 2.3; Fabulae 82–83); Ovid identifies Pelops as Niobe's brother and Tantalus as her father (Metamorphoses 6.172, 6.404–411)
The Magnesians credited their ancient rock image of the Mother of the Gods to Broteas, son of Tantalus (Description of Greece 3.22.4)
Oenomaus, son of Mars and Asterope (Fabulae 84)
Daughter and marriage prize of the king of Pisa (Epitome 2.4–5; Fabulae 84)
Myrtilus, son of Hermes and charioteer of Oenomaus (Epitome 2.6)
Pelops won Hippodamia in Oenomaus' chariot contest (Epitome 2.4–9; Fabulae 84)
Pelops cast Myrtilus into the sea, but the motive differs: attempted assault in Apollodorus, a repudiated payment in Hyginus (Epitome 2.8; Fabulae 84)
The rival Pelopid brothers of the golden lamb and the accursed banquet (Epitome 2.10–14; Fabulae 86–88; Description of Greece 2.18.1)
Aerope gave Thyestes the hidden golden lamb (Epitome 2.10–11; Fabulae 86)
At Hippodamia's instigation, Atreus and Thyestes killed Chrysippus (Fabulae 85)
At Hippodamia's instigation, Atreus and Thyestes killed Chrysippus (Fabulae 85)
The daughter through whom the oracle promised Thyestes an avenger (Fabulae 87–88)
Born from Thyestes' union with his own daughter (Epitome 2.14; Fabulae 87–88)
Pelopia exposed the infant, who was nursed by a she-goat (Fabulae 87)
Aegisthus killed Atreus and restored Thyestes (Epitome 2.14; Fabulae 88)
Son of Thyestes in Apollodorus; one of two fathers reported by Pausanias (Epitome 2.15–16; Description of Greece 2.22.3)
The alternative father reported for Clytemnestra's first husband (Description of Greece 2.22.3)
Clytemnestra's husband before Agamemnon (Epitome 2.15–16; Description of Greece 2.18.2, 2.22.3)
Agamemnon killed Tantalus and his newborn child before marrying Clytemnestra (Epitome 2.15–16; Description of Greece 2.18.2)
Explicitly son of Atreus in the ship catalogue and Hyginus' king list (Epitome 3.12; Fabulae 124)
Agamemnon, son of Atreus and Aerope (Epitome 3.12)
Menelaus, son of Atreus and Aerope (Epitome 3.12)
Menelaus, son of Atreus and Aerope (Epitome 3.12)

The Spartan royal marriage at the center of the Trojan War

Principal killer in Homer; joint killer with Clytemnestra in Apollodorus and Hyginus
A direct joint killer in Epitome 6.23 and Fabulae 117; Homer makes her the accomplice of Aegisthus
The son who avenged Agamemnon and inherited Argos
Son of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra (Epitome 2.16; Fabulae 119)
Daughter of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra (Epitome 2.16; Fabulae 122)
Agamemnon's daughter in Apollodorus and sister of Orestes in Hyginus (Epitome 2.16, 3.21–22; Fabulae 120–121)
Sent to Aulis by Clytemnestra as Agamemnon's daughter (Epitome 2.16, 3.21–22)
The Argive tradition made Helen her mother and Theseus her father (Description of Greece 2.22.6–7)
The one daughter named by both catalogues (Iliad 9.141–148; Epitome 2.16)
Among the children born in Agamemnon and Clytemnestra's household (Epitome 2.16)
The Spartan heiress and only child of Helen (Odyssey 4.1–14; Epitome 3.3; Description of Greece 2.18.6)
Helen's only child in Homer, left behind at Sparta in Apollodorus (Odyssey 4.1–14; Epitome 3.3)
Daughter of Aegisthus and later mother of Penthilus (Epitome 6.25; Description of Greece 2.18.6)
Erigone, daughter of Aegisthus and Clytemnestra (Epitome 6.25)
Electra saved the infant Orestes and sent him to Strophius (Epitome 6.24; Fabulae 117)
Companion in the Mycenaean revenge and the voyage to Tauris
The vengeance for Agamemnon celebrated across the surviving traditions
The matricide that brought pursuit by the Furies (Epitome 6.25; Fabulae 119)
Orestes arranged their marriage; Pausanias records two sons (Epitome 6.28; Description of Greece 2.16.7)
Wife and mother of Tisamenus; Apollodorus also reports Erigone as an alternative (Epitome 6.28; Description of Greece 2.18.6)
Alternative wife and mother of Tisamenus in Apollodorus; mother of a separate son Penthilus in Pausanias
Named among the male Titans born from Earth and Sky (Theogony 132–138; Bibliotheca 1.1.3)
Hyginus' divergent genealogy makes Memory a daughter of Jove and Clymene (Fabulae Preface, Grant p. 30)
Parents of Leto and Asteria (Theogony 404–411; Bibliotheca 1.2.2)
Parents of Helios, Selene and Eos; Hyginus names Aethra instead of Theia
Their nine-night union produced the nine Muses (Theogony 53–67, 915–917; Bibliotheca 1.3.1)
Parents of Aphrodite in the Homeric and Apollodoran genealogy

At the first Zeus the cloud-gatherer begat Dardanus, whom he loved above all his children by mortal women (Hom. Il. 20.215, 20.304-305); son of Electra, daughter of Atlas, by Zeus (Apollod. 3.12.1; Hyg. Fab. 155, 275; Astr. 2.21.5)

Dardanus in turn begat a son, king Erichthonius, who became richest of mortal men (Hom. Il. 20.219-220); Dardanus had sons Ilus and Erichthonius, and Erichthonius succeeded to the kingdom (Apollod. 3.12.2)
Erichthonius begat Tros to be king among the Trojans (Hom. Il. 20.230); Erichthonius married Astyoche, daughter of Simoeis, and begat Tros, who called the country Troy after himself (Apollod. 3.12.2)
From Tros three peerless sons were born, Ilus, Assaracus and godlike Ganymedes (Hom. Il. 20.231-232); Tros by Callirrhoe, daughter of Scamander, begat Ilus, Assaracus and Ganymede (Apollod. 3.12.2)
From Tros three peerless sons were born, Ilus, Assaracus and godlike Ganymedes (Hom. Il. 20.231-232); Tros by Callirrhoe begat Ilus, Assaracus and Ganymede (Apollod. 3.12.2)

Third of the peerless sons of Tros, fairest of mortal men, caught up to be cupbearer of Zeus (Hom. Il. 20.231-235; Apollod. 3.12.2); Hyginus instead calls Ganymede a son of Erichthonius (Fab. 271) or of Assaracus (Fab. 224)
Ilus again begat a son, peerless Laomedon (Hom. Il. 20.236); Ilus married Eurydice, daughter of Adrastus, and begat Laomedon (Apollod. 3.12.3)

Laomedon begat Tithonus and Priam and Clytius, and Hicetaon (Hom. Il. 20.237-238); first of the five sons of Laomedon (Apollod. 3.12.3); Apollodorus elsewhere also knows a Tithonus born to Cephalus and the Dawn in Syria (Apollod. 3.14.3)
Rise, thou son of Laomedon (Hom. Il. 3.250; 20.237); Podarces, son of Laomedon, was ransomed and called Priam (Apollod. 3.12.3, 3.12.5; cf. 2.6.4); Priam, son of Laomedon (Hyg. Fab. 89, 91)
And Assaracus begat Capys (Hom. Il. 20.239); Assaracus had by his wife Hieromneme, daughter of Simoeis, a son Capys (Apollod. 3.12.2)

Assaracus begat Capys, and he Anchises (Hom. Il. 20.239); Capys had by his wife Themiste, daughter of Ilus, a son Anchises (Apollod. 3.12.2); Hyginus instead calls Anchises a son of Assaracus (Fab. 270)

Aeneas, whom fair Aphrodite conceived to Anchises amid the spurs of Ida (Hom. Il. 2.819-821; 5.247-248; 20.208-209); Cytherea bore Aeneas to the hero Anchises on the peaks of Ida (Hes. Theog. 1008-1010); Apollod. 3.12.2; Hyg. Fab. 94

His mother is Aphrodite, who flung her white arms about her dear son to shelter him (Hom. Il. 2.820-821; 5.247-248, 5.311-315); Cytherea bore Aeneas, joined in sweet love with Anchises (Hes. Theog. 1008-1010); she bore him Aeneas and Lyrus (Apollod. 3.12.2); by Anchises Venus conceived Aeneas (Hyg. Fab. 94)
Hector son of Priam (Hom. Il. 15.596-598 and throughout); the first son born to Hecuba was Hector (Apollod. 3.12.5); the mother of great Hector, once the wife of Priam (Ov. Met. 13.508-515)

Hecabe led the lament: Hector, far dearest to my heart of all my children (Hom. Il. 22.405-407, 24.747-748); the first son born to her was Hector (Apollod. 3.12.5); Hector was child of Hecuba, who was daughter of Dymas (Ov. Met. 11.761-763)

Priam called aloud to his sons, chiding Helenus and Paris (Hom. Il. 24.248-251); the second babe of Priam and Hecuba, exposed after the firebrand dream and acknowledged again (Apollod. 3.12.5); Alexander Paris, son of Priam and Hecuba (Hyg. Fab. 91, 270)
When a second babe was about to be born Hecuba dreamed she had brought forth a firebrand (Apollod. 3.12.5); Alexander Paris, son of Priam and Hecuba (Hyg. Fab. 91, 270)

The comeliest of the daughters of Priam, even Cassandra (Hom. Il. 13.365-366; Od. 11.421-422); Hecuba gave birth to daughters Creusa, Laodice, Polyxena and Cassandra (Apollod. 3.12.5); Cassandra, daughter of Priam and Hecuba (Hyg. Fab. 93)
After Hector, Hecuba gave birth to daughters Creusa, Laodice, Polyxena and Cassandra (Apollod. 3.12.5); Cassandra, daughter of Priam and Hecuba (Hyg. Fab. 93)

He called to him Hecabe his wife (Hom. Il. 24.193-194; cf. 22.234-235); Priam married a second wife, Hecuba, daughter of Dymas or, as some say, of Cisseus (Apollod. 3.12.5); once the wife of Priam (Ov. Met. 13.508-515); Hecuba, wife of Priam (Hyg. Fab. 91, 111, 256)

Dawn rose from her couch from beside lordly Tithonus (Hom. Il. 11.1; Od. 5.1); Eos bore to Tithonus brazen-crested Memnon and the lord Emathion (Hes. Theog. 984-985); the Dawn snatched away Tithonus for love and bore him two sons in Ethiopia (Apollod. 3.12.4); Tithonus, husband of Aurora (Hyg. Fab. 270; cf. 189)

Hector sought his peerless wife Andromache in his halls, and she avows him her stalwart husband (Hom. Il. 6.370-374, 8.186-190, 24.723-745); Hector married Andromache, daughter of Eetion (Apollod. 3.12.6)

A goddess couched with a mortal man amid the spurs of Ida (Hom. Il. 2.820-821); Cytherea with the beautiful crown was joined in sweet love with the hero Anchises (Hes. Theog. 1008-1010); Aphrodite met Anchises in love's dalliance (Apollod. 3.12.2); Venus is said to have loved Anchises and to have lain with him (Hyg. Fab. 94)

Alexander, lord of fair-haired Helen, whom Aphrodite leads back to his bed (Hom. Il. 3.328-329, 3.421-447); Alexander carried off Helen from Sparta (Apollod. Epit. 3.1; 3.12.6); Alexander Paris, whom Helen followed (Hyg. Fab. 270; cf. 91); Homer is cited for their first union on the island of Cranae (Paus. 3.22.1)

Sarpedon, leader of the Lycian allies, chides Hector to stand fast and stings him to the heart (Hom. Il. 5.471-496); he led the glorious allies in Hector's assault on the Achaean wall (Hom. Il. 12.101-104, 12.290-330)

Hecuba bore to Priam the daughters Creusa, Laodice, Polyxena, Cassandra (Apollod. 3.12.5); King Priam's daughter pleads at the tomb (Ov. Met. 13.439-480); Polyxena, daughter of Priam, sacrificed at Achilles' tomb (Hyg. Fab. 110)
Among the daughters Hecuba bore (Apollod. 3.12.5); torn from her mother's breast for the sacrifice (Ov. Met. 13.439-480)
First of the daughters Hecuba bore to Priam (Apollod. 3.12.5); Creusa in the catalogue of Priam's children (Hyg. Fab. 90)
Hecuba bore the daughters Creusa, Laodice, Polyxena, Cassandra (Apollod. 3.12.5)
Creusa is said to have been the wife of Aeneas, saved from slavery by the Mother of the Gods and Aphrodite (Paus. 10.26.1)
His daughter Hesione, exposed for the sea monster (Apollod. 2.5.9; cf. 3.12.3); the king's daughter chained to the rocks (Ov. Met. 11.194-217); Hesione, daughter of Laomedon (Hyg. Fab. 31, 89, 97)
Among the sons of Priam (Hom. Il. 22.233-234, 24.248-251); Hecuba bore sons, Deiphobus among them (Apollod. 3.12.5); Deiphobus, son of Priam (Hyg. Fab. 90, 240)
Brethren born of Hecabe and Priam (Hom. Il. 22.233-234); Hecuba bore sons, Deiphobus among them (Apollod. 3.12.5)
After Alexander's death Deiphobus was preferred over Helenus to marry Helen (Apollod. Epit. 5.9); Deiphobus counted among the husbands Helen's hand undid (Hyg. Fab. 240)
Menelaus slew Deiphobus and led away Helen to the ships (Apollod. Epit. 5.22)

Helenus, son of Priam, far the best of augurs (Hom. Il. 6.76); among Hecuba's sons (Apollod. 3.12.5); the Phrygian seer who ruled mimic Troy (Ov. Met. 13.1015-1078, 15.498-667); Helenus, son of Priam (Hyg. Fab. 90, 128); Helenus the son of Priam (Paus. 2.23.6)
